reading.body:
Sega v. Accolade holds that copying a program in full to study it is fair use when that is the only way to reach the unprotected functional elements inside and there is a legitimate reason to reach them.

The decision turns on purpose rather than completeness. Accolade copied entire programs, and the court still found fair use because the copy was an intermediate step toward interoperability, a legitimate and narrow aim. The doctrine that grew from it, intermediate copying, judges the copy by what it was for, not by the fact that it was whole.

That is the line AI training cases now argue over. Ingestion necessarily makes copies before any output exists, so the question becomes whether training is the kind of legitimate purpose Accolade protected. The data records 90 live cases citing this precedent, including suits against OpenAI and Suno, which shows the argument is in active use rather than settled.

What the data does not supply is any ruling on whether training on copyrighted works is that same legitimate purpose. The case's own limits note that producing a competing creative work is contested ground, and the live cases are citations, not outcomes. The precedent establishes the framework, not the answer.
